items.q: Why can one slow downstream service take down every upstream service even when CPU utilization is still low?
items.a:
The root cause is that [[r:threads/connections are held while waiting for the downstream service]].

- Service A has a Tomcat pool of 200 threads, and every request calls B
- B normally responds in 20ms → threads are released quickly (~10,000 req/s)
- B slows to 5s → each thread is held for 5s → A's throughput collapses to ~40 req/s

A fails not because of CPU exhaustion, but because of [[r:thread starvation]] — it has no concurrent execution units left.

A [[r:retry storm]] compounds the problem: A times out calling B and retries; B is lagging rather than dead → retries double B's load → B fails completely → A retries aggressively → B cannot recover even after a restart.

:::deep
This is called a [[o:metastable failure]]: the system becomes trapped in a bad state and cannot escape *even after the original trigger is gone*.

Two reinforcing loops are at work:
- *retry amplification* — retries multiply load at every layer; across three layers, the amplification is x8
- *load-induced slowdown* — higher load makes the system slower (GC, lock contention, context switching) → more timeouts → more retries

Recovery requires [[g:actively shedding load]], not merely waiting for the system to heal itself.
:::

items.q: How should timeouts be configured?
items.a:
Timeouts should consume one [[g:end-to-end deadline budget]], not form a fixed hierarchy in which every outer timeout is greater than the sum of every inner timeout. Sequential calls and retries consume time cumulatively; parallel branches consume the longest branch plus coordination overhead. At each hop, derive a local timeout from the remaining deadline while preserving time to cancel work, release resources, and return a useful response.
BoundaryFailure it bounds
pool acquisitionwaiting for a connection/thread/permit before any I/O starts
DNS/connect/TLSestablishing the connection
request/write and response/reada peer that accepts a connection but stalls mid-protocol
database statement/lockserver-side work that can outlive an abandoned HTTP request
overall deadlinethe maximum time the caller is willing to wait for the whole operation
edge deadline: T+3000ms
  parallel fraud and limits checks: each receives remaining budget, capped locally
  sequential PSP call: starts only if budget includes call + cleanup margin
  retry: allowed only when eligibility, backoff, and another attempt fit the deadline
:::deep Propagate an absolute deadline when protocols support it (gRPC does); relative “3 seconds from now” values at every hop accidentally recreate the budget. Cancellation must reach the HTTP client, executor and database driver where possible—timing out the caller while the query continues still consumes the pool. Choose values from latency distributions by operation and failure mode, including cold paths and dependency degradation. Define an acceptable false-timeout rate and test it; “p99.9 plus a margin” is a starting method, not a universal formula. Observe timeout reason, remaining budget, canceled work and late completions without turning raw URLs or IDs into high-cardinality metrics. Retry policy is covered in (25-microservice.01-cascading-failure-retry-storm.q5). :::

items.q: Circuit breakers: the three states and key Resilience4j parameters
items.a:
A circuit breaker is a local admission policy around one dependency/operation: - [[b:CLOSED]] permits calls and records classified outcomes over its window. - [[b:OPEN]] rejects calls until the open-state wait policy permits another evaluation; a fallback is optional and must be semantically safe. - [[b:HALF_OPEN]] admits a bounded set of probes, then closes or reopens according to their classified results. 
// Illustrative values only—derive them from this operation's traffic and SLO.
CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
    .slidingWindowSize(100)
    .minimumNumberOfCalls(20)
    .failureRateThreshold(50)            // open at or above 50%
    .slowCallRateThreshold(80)             // open at or above 80%
    .slowCallDurationThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(800))
    .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
    .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(10)
    .build();
Classify which exceptions/statuses count as failures, which are ignored, and what “slow” means for this endpoint. A validation rejection should not normally trip a dependency breaker. `minimumNumberOfCalls` protects low-volume windows from computing a rate on too little data, but it also delays reaction; choose count- or time-based windows from traffic shape. :::deep Breakers are commonly per process/pod, so instances can disagree. Centralizing breaker state adds coordination and another dependency; use it only for a demonstrated requirement. Protect recovery from synchronized probes with bounded HALF_OPEN traffic, jittered/open durations where supported, dependency capacity limits and gradual ramp-up. A fallback is not automatically resilience: stale data, an empty success, or a second dependency can violate the contract or create another cascade. Expose breaker state, rejected/slow/classified calls and fallback outcome at bounded cardinality. The documented Resilience4j defaults are not a substitute for a load/degradation test. :::

items.q: Bulkheads: semaphore vs thread pool, and what changes with virtual threads?
items.a:
A bulkhead partitions concurrency or execution capacity by downstream dependency so one slow dependency cannot consume every shared resource.

Resilience4j provides two distinct mechanisms:

- [[b:`SemaphoreBulkhead`]] limits simultaneous calls and executes on the caller's thread.
- [[b:`FixedThreadPoolBulkhead`]] submits work to a dedicated fixed pool with a bounded queue, isolating both threads and queued work.

A thread-pool bulkhead does [[r:not]] impose a hard execution timeout. Compose a separate `TimeLimiter`/client deadline and make cancellation effective in the underlying call.

With virtual threads, a semaphore is often the simpler way to cap downstream concurrency, but a separate executor can still be useful for ownership, queueing, or legacy isolation—choose from failure behavior, not fashion.

:::deep
A circuit breaker reacts after enough outcomes are recorded; a bulkhead limits concurrency immediately. A rate limiter controls starts over time; a timeout bounds waiting/execution time. They solve different dimensions and should be configured from one end-to-end deadline and overload policy.

Little's Law, `L = λW`, gives a starting estimate only when the system is stable and units align. Use observed arrival rate and service-time distribution, leave headroom for variance, then load-test rejection and recovery.

For a downstream with long-tail latency, sizing from the mean alone creates a queue precisely during incidents.

Record permitted, rejected, queued, timed-out, cancelled, and completed calls per dependency. A limit is useful only if rejection maps to a deliberate response such as fallback, `429`/`503`, or bounded retry—not an unobserved exception loop.
:::

items.q: Safe retries: jitter and retry budgets
items.a:
A safe retry policy classifies the operation, failure, deadline, and shared load before choosing attempts. 
IntervalFunction backoff = IntervalFunction.ofExponentialRandomBackoff(
    Duration.ofMillis(100), 2.0, 0.5); // example values; derive from the service contract
- Retry only failures explicitly classified as transient and only when repeating the operation is safe. An idempotency key/unique business key is required for retrying a money-creating `POST`. - Give every attempt a timeout inside one absolute end-to-end deadline. Stop when remaining time cannot support another useful attempt. - Use exponential backoff and usually jitter under distributed load so clients do not synchronize; also honor a valid `Retry-After`. - Bound attempts and total retry traffic. A retry budget can cap retries relative to successful/original traffic and close when the dependency is unhealthy. - Do not treat all `4xx` or `5xx` alike: policy may retry `408`, `429`, selected conflicts, or some `5xx`, while many validation/authentication failures are permanent. Define it per API. :::deep There is no universally correct decorator order. If the circuit breaker wraps the whole retry, it records one final outcome per logical operation; if retry wraps the breaker, the breaker observes each failed attempt and may open sooner. Per-attempt versus whole-operation timeout placement changes cancellation and metrics similarly. Write the desired semantics first—what counts as a breaker failure, which layer owns retries, how many attempts can occur across the call chain, and whether a fallback is safe—then compose and test the actual library decorators. Avoid retries at multiple layers unless a propagated budget prevents multiplicative amplification. Record original calls, attempts, successes-after-retry, exhausted/rejected retries, added latency, and downstream load. If retries rarely recover but materially amplify incidents, remove or narrow them. :::

items.q: Load shedding — the last line of defense
items.a:
[[b:Load shedding]] rejects lower-value or excess work before it consumes the scarce resource, preserving useful throughput and bounded latency for admitted work.

Place admission at the earliest boundary that knows both cost and priority: gateway, per-endpoint limiter, worker queue, or dependency bulkhead.

Use direct saturation signals such as in-flight work, queue age/depth, available permits/connections and deadline-miss probability. CPU and p99 are valuable confirmation but may react after queues have already grown.

Define overload classes and fairness: reserve capacity for critical operations, cap noisy tenants, and ensure a large expensive request does not count like a cheap lookup merely because both are “one request.”

:::tip Rejection contract
Use `429` for a client/quota policy and `503` for temporary service capacity when those meanings fit the API.
:::

Return `Retry-After` only with a retry policy the server can support; clients still need jitter, a deadline and a retry budget. For non-idempotent work, never invite an automatic retry without an idempotency contract.
:::deep
Fixed concurrency/queue limits are simple and auditable. Adaptive limiters can adjust from latency or gradient signals as workload cost changes, but they are control loops—not a way to eliminate maximum bounds, minimum capacity, priority rules or tuning.

Test stability, cold start, low traffic, dependency slowdown and correlated bursts; expose the chosen limit and rejection reason.

Shedding after work enters an unbounded queue is too late. Couple admission with bounded queues, cancellation and backpressure so rejected/expired work releases resources. Compare this incident card with the canonical overload workflow in (10-system-design-rate-limit.surviving-high-load.q2).
:::

items.q: Connection-pool sizing: why is a larger pool not always better?
items.a:
A database connection pool is an admission-control boundary as well as a reuse mechanism. Too many active queries can increase CPU scheduling, lock/latch contention, memory, I/O queueing, and cache churn, so adding connections can reduce throughput and worsen tail latency.

Do not use `(cores × 2) + spindles` or “10–20 connections” as a universal answer. Start from:

- the database's measured concurrent-query capacity for this workload and its CPU/I/O/lock profile;
- an aggregate connection budget after reserving administration, migrations, replicas/HA, background jobs, and other applications;
- per-instance traffic, query service-time distribution, transaction hold time, autoscaling maximum, and acceptable pool wait;
- separate budgets for interactive and batch traffic when one can starve the other.

:::deep
Load-test increasing concurrency while plotting throughput, p95/p99 query latency, DB CPU/I/O/saturation, locks, pool active/pending/timeouts, and application SLO.

Select the smallest pool that meets peak throughput with recovery headroom; validate failure and autoscaling scenarios, not only steady state.

Little's Law can estimate needed in-flight work from arrival rate and observed hold time in a stable system, but transactions, burstiness, and long tails require headroom and measurement. A pool queue absorbs only a bounded burst; it must not become an unbounded latency buffer.

Connections also consume server and client memory/state, but the cost is engine/version/configuration-specific. Measure the selected PostgreSQL/MySQL/cloud product instead of quoting a fixed megabytes-per-connection value.
:::

items.q: Aggregate connections across instances exceed max_connections
items.a:
The budget is fleet-wide: `max replicas × pool size`, plus jobs, migrations, admin tools, and other services, must fit below the database limit with failover/recovery reserve. Autoscaling can therefore exhaust connections even while each pod's pool looks healthy.

First control demand: cap replica count and per-pod pools coherently, shorten transactions, separate batch traffic, shed excess work, and raise database capacity only after measuring.

A connection proxy/pooler such as RDS Proxy or PgBouncer is [[o:one option]], not an automatic requirement; it helps when many client connections are mostly idle or churn, but it cannot create database query capacity.

:::deep
Proxy semantics matter. Session pooling preserves a backend connection for a client session and multiplexes less.

Transaction pooling reassigns a backend after each transaction, so arbitrary session state—temporary tables, session-level `SET`, some advisory-lock/listen behavior, and driver assumptions—may not survive.

“Prepared statements must always be disabled” is outdated and too broad.

PgBouncer version/configuration and protocol matter: modern releases can track protocol-level named prepared statements when configured, while SQL-level `PREPARE`/`DEALLOCATE`, session state, DDL changes, and particular drivers need explicit compatibility tests.

RDS Proxy can pin sessions for operations that prevent multiplexing, reducing its benefit.

Test transactions, prepared statements, failover, credential rotation, cancellation, idle/maximum lifetime, and observability through the exact proxy mode before rollout. Monitor client connections, backend connections, pinning/multiplex ratio, wait, transaction latency, and rejected connections.
:::

items.q: HikariCP: critical parameters
items.a:
maximumPoolSize: 20          # example only; must fit the fleet-wide DB budget
connectionTimeout: 3000     # maximum wait to borrow from the pool
validationTimeout: 1000     # must be less than connectionTimeout
maxLifetime: 1740000        # maximum connection age; below infrastructure max-age limit
keepaliveTime: 120000       # ping an idle connection; must be less than maxLifetime
leakDetectionThreshold: 60000 # logs a possible long checkout; zero disables
- `maximumPoolSize` is the maximum total connections, including idle and in-use; derive it with all replicas. - `connectionTimeout` bounds pool wait, not JDBC connect, socket, statement, or transaction time. Configure those deadlines in their own layers. - `maxLifetime` retires connections by age after they return to the pool; set it a little below a known database/proxy/network maximum connection lifetime, with jitter handled by Hikari. - `keepaliveTime` tests an idle connection to prevent infrastructure idle expiry and must be lower than `maxLifetime`. Do not confuse idle timeout with maximum age. - `leakDetectionThreshold` logs when a connection remains checked out longer than the threshold. It signals a [[o:possible leak]], not proof that code never returns it; a legitimate long transaction also triggers it. :::deep Hikari recommends considering a fixed-size pool (`minimumIdle` left unset so it follows the maximum) for responsiveness, but that is not a universal mandate. An elastic pool can reduce idle connections at the cost of creating them during demand; choose from database budget, connection-establishment cost, workload burst, and platform behavior. `idleTimeout` applies only when `minimumIdle` is below `maximumPoolSize`. Keepalive occurs only on idle connections, while an in-use connection is never retired at `maxLifetime` until returned. This distinction prevents the common mistake of setting `maxLifetime` from an infrastructure *idle* timeout while omitting keepalive. Monitor active, idle, pending, acquire duration/timeouts, usage duration, creation failures, and DB-side sessions. A short `connectionTimeout` is useful only when rejection/degradation is deliberate and clients do not immediately retry into another storm. :::

items.q: Thread pools: the queueCapacity gotcha
items.a:
The actual `ThreadPoolExecutor` admission order is [[g:core → queue → max → reject]], not the intuitive core → max → queue. 
running < core?        → create a new thread
else queue not full?   → PUT IN QUEUE (do not create a thread!)
else thread < max?     → create a new thread
else                   → REJECT
[[r:The trap]]: with a large `queueCapacity`—and the default `LinkedBlockingQueue` capacity is `Integer.MAX_VALUE`—the queue never fills → the pool [[r:never grows beyond corePoolSize]] → `maxPoolSize` becomes meaningless. → use a bounded queue with `CallerRunsPolicy`. It provides natural backpressure: the task runs on the calling thread, which automatically slows task submission. :::deep To "scale threads first and queue later," use `SynchronousQueue` or a custom queue that overrides `offer()`, as Tomcat does with `TaskQueue`. CallerRunsPolicy has a downside on a web server: it consumes a Tomcat request thread → fewer threads remain to accept new requests → backpressure propagates to the client. That can be intentional, but a latency-critical path should consider failing fast with 503 instead. :::

items.q: Virtual threads remove the I/O-bound bottleneck—and introduce new traps
items.a:
Virtual threads remove the need to use a small platform-thread pool merely because blocked OS threads are expensive. They do not remove any downstream limit.

- A supported blocking operation parks and unmounts the virtual thread, allowing its carrier to run another task.
- On JDK 21–23, blocking under a `synchronized` monitor could pin the carrier. JDK 24 removed monitor-related pinning; native/foreign calls and class-initialization edge cases can still hold it.
- CPU-bound work remains limited by cores.
- Cheap threads remove an accidental admission limit: thousands of requests can now wait on a 20-connection pool or flood a partner unless concurrency is bounded explicitly.

:::deep
Do not quote a universal “6× improvement” or a fixed stack cost. Measure throughput, RSS, allocation, carrier utilization, pending connections, queue depth, and p99 under the same container limits and workload.

Use one virtual thread per task, then place a semaphore or the resource's own pool at each scarce dependency. Give waiting an absolute deadline and shed work before the queue consumes the latency budget.

On JDK 21–23, the old pinned-thread diagnostic and JFR event can help; `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads` was removed in JDK 24, so use current JFR/thread-dump evidence instead.

The runtime details are covered in (01-java-core-jvm.concurrency.q1) and the JDK 25 coding API in (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q4).
:::

items.q: The dual-write problem — why is this code subtly wrong?
items.a:
@Transactional
public void placeOrder(Order order) {
    orderRepository.save(order);        // write to the DB transaction
    messageBroker.publish(orderEvent);  // publish to the broker
}
The database and broker are [[r:not part of the same transaction]]. `@Transactional` covers only the database. - if the database commits and the process crashes before publish → the [[r:event is lost]] - if publish succeeds but the database transaction then rolls back → downstream consumers process an order that does not exist [[r:Do not solve this with 2PC/XA]]: it is slow and fragile, and holds blocking locks across systems. :::deep 2PC is generally avoided because the prepare phase holds locks on every participant until commit. If the coordinator dies mid-protocol, participants can remain "in-doubt" and retain locks indefinitely → destroying throughput and introducing a single point of failure. Reversing the order and publishing first is still wrong: the problem is *not ordering*, but the *lack of atomicity across two media*. The reliable approach is to place both writes in one transactional medium—the database—and relay from there. That is the [[g:Outbox]] pattern. :::

items.q: Transactional Outbox: polling vs CDC
Sagas: orchestration vs choreography and compensation traps
items.a:
A saga is a sequence of local transactions; when a step fails, completed work is reversed with a [[g:compensating transaction]].

[[b:Choreography]] is event-driven and loosely coupled, but it can turn into a "pinball" flow that is difficult to debug. Beyond four or five steps, prefer [[b:orchestration]] with an explicit state machine such as Temporal or Camunda.

[[r:Compensation traps in fintech]]:
- [[r:Compensation ≠ rollback]]: after debiting money and sending an SMS, you cannot unsend the SMS → design a semantic refund by crediting the amount back, not by "un-debiting" it
- [[r:Pivot transaction]]: after crossing the pivot point, such as disbursing funds externally, compensation is impossible → after the pivot, only retry forward
- [[r:Compensation can also fail]] → it must be retried and idempotent

:::deep
A [[g:semantic lock]] reduces user-visible inconsistency between a completed step and unfinished compensation. Keep an explicit intermediate state such as `PENDING_CONFIRM` instead of immediately changing the effective balance, and finalize it only when the entire saga succeeds.
:::

items.q: Where does eventual consistency hurt?
items.a:
[[r:Read-after-write is not guaranteed]]: a user deposits money and refreshes immediately, but the balance has not updated because the replica or projection has not caught up.

Mitigations include:
- [[g:read-your-writes]] consistency by routing reads to the primary for N seconds
- an [[g:optimistic UI]] that shows "processing"
- distinguishing data that [[o:must be strongly consistent]], such as balances and limits, from data that [[o:can be eventually consistent]], such as history and statistics

:::deep
Consistency is a spectrum that includes read-your-writes, [[b:monotonic reads]]—never observing data move backward to an older value—and causal consistency.

Many fintech UX bugs violate monotonic reads: the user sees a new balance, refreshes, and sees the old value after being routed to a different replica.

Fix this with a [[g:version token]]: after a write, return an LSN/version to the client; the next read sends that token, and the server routes it to a replica that has caught up to at least that version.
:::

items.q: What does “exactly once” guarantee, and where does that guarantee end?
items.a:
“Exactly once” is meaningful only after defining the [[o:scope, observer, failure model, and side effects]]. It is wrong both to promise universal exactly-once delivery and to dismiss every exactly-once guarantee as a myth.

Kafka can provide scope-bound exactly-once processing: idempotent producers and transactions atomically commit consumed offsets with produced records, and consumers using `read_committed` avoid aborted writes.

Kafka Streams' exactly-once processing mode applies within Kafka-managed input/state/output boundaries. It does not automatically include a PostgreSQL commit, email, payment-provider call, or arbitrary REST effect.

For an effect outside that transaction boundary, crashes around “effect succeeded / acknowledgement failed” create ambiguity.

Use a local transaction with inbox/outbox, stable operation/event IDs, unique constraints, idempotent receiver semantics, and reconciliation so repeated delivery produces one business outcome.

:::deep
Separate terms:

- **delivery:** how often transport presents a record;
- **processing attempt:** how often handler code executes;
- **business effect:** what a declared observer can see in durable state.

At-least-once delivery can produce effectively-once business effects when the effect is idempotent and deduplication is atomic with it. A transactional system can give exactly-once visibility within its own boundary even though networks still retry messages.

Ask vendors which resources share the transaction, how failover/fencing works, what consumers must configure, and what happens when an external effect is introduced.

The practical design question is: “If this operation runs twice or its outcome is unknown, how do we detect, converge, and reconcile?”
:::

items.q: Backpressure and queue buildup: RabbitMQ vs Kafka
items.a:
When producers outpace consumers, the queue grows → end-to-end latency rises and broker memory pressure increases.

- [[b:RabbitMQ]]: `prefetch` (QoS) matters because an unlimited value lets one consumer take all available work while others starve. Use roughly 10–50 for lightweight tasks or 1 for heavy tasks. Lazy/quorum queues persist messages to disk to avoid OOM. Measure pressure with [[o:queue depth]]
- [[b:Kafka]]: as a disk-backed log, it does not run out of memory merely because messages accumulate, but rising [[o:consumer lag]] means increasingly stale data

:::deep
Optimal prefetch is approximately throughput × round-trip time, an inverse application of Little's Law. Too low and the consumer waits for acknowledgments; too high and work becomes imbalanced, with many unacknowledged messages stranded when a consumer dies.

For Kafka, alert on the *derivative of lag*—whether it is growing or shrinking—not only its absolute value. Partition count is the consumer group's [[r:scaling ceiling]]: a group cannot have more active consumers than partitions.
:::

items.q: Message ordering under horizontal scale
items.a:
Ordering is a scoped guarantee. Kafka orders records in one partition; RabbitMQ preserves queue delivery order under its documented conditions, but multiple consumers, redelivery and application concurrency can change the order in which side effects complete. Define the business scope first—usually one account/order/aggregate—not “all events globally.” - Choose a stable key and keep every event that shares an ordering invariant on the same partition/consumer lane. A hot key limits parallelism, and changing partition count or key logic needs a migration plan. - With Kafka, producer idempotence preserves order for supported configurations; retries with idempotence disabled and more than one in-flight request can reorder batches. Do not copy the old blanket rule “always set max in-flight to 1”—verify the client/version contract. - A rebalance or ack/offset failure can reprocess records. Consumer idempotency handles duplicates but does not by itself reject a late older event; use an aggregate version/sequence and an atomic conditional update when stale events would corrupt state. - Parallel handlers may finish out of order even when delivery was ordered. Commit/ack only after the intended side effect and define how poison messages or slow keys affect progress. :::deep RabbitMQ single-active-consumer can serialize consumption with failover; consistent-hash routing can shard by key, but redelivery still requires idempotency. Kafka partition order is broker append order, not necessarily event-time order from distributed producers. If producers can race, allocate the sequence at the state owner or make the consumer compare versions. Global total order usually destroys throughput and still does not make external side effects atomic. State the narrow invariant and test producer retry, rebalance, duplicate, delayed event, key migration and DLQ replay. Broker-specific details live in (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q4). **Ordering is a producer key plus a consumer-side aggregate sequence:** 
// every event for one order resolves to the same partition
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("order-events", orderId, eventJson));
-- consumer transaction: accept exactly the next event for this aggregate
UPDATE order_projection
   SET status=:status, last_seq=:seq
 WHERE order_id=:orderId AND last_seq=:seq-1;
-- update count 1: apply side effects and commit offset with the transaction
-- update count 0 + seq <= last_seq: duplicate/replay, acknowledge safely
-- update count 0 + seq > last_seq+1: gap, pause/retry/reconcile; do not skip it
Keep producer idempotence enabled with `acks=all`, but do not confuse broker retry ordering with end-to-end processing. - **Benefit:** unrelated aggregates scale across partitions while each order stays serial. - **Cost:** a hot key is bounded by one partition, re-keying can split history, and DLQ replay still needs the sequence guard. :::

items.q: Poison messages and DLQs
items.a:
A [[b:poison message]] repeatedly fails for a reason retries cannot heal: unreadable bytes/schema, invalid data, an unsupported version, or a deterministic handler bug. A transient dependency timeout is different; classify failures before choosing retry or quarantine.

Use bounded attempts, exponential backoff with jitter and an overall age/deadline. Delayed retry topics/queues or broker features keep the main consumer lane from sleeping, but they change ordering and increase operational state.

After the policy is exhausted, quarantine the original payload plus source topic/queue, partition/offset or message ID, headers/schema version, first/last failure time, attempt count, producer identity and a sanitized error classification.

:::tip A DLQ is a workflow, not storage
Alert on rate and oldest age; assign ownership and retention. Provide an audited replay tool that can inspect, patch/transform when authorized, choose a target version, throttle traffic and record who replayed what.
:::

Replay must pass through an idempotent consumer and may need the original key/order lane.
:::deep
For batch handlers, isolate or bisect the failing record when the broker/framework supports partial acknowledgement; blindly retrying a large batch reprocesses good work and can block a partition.

Never deserialize untrusted DLQ content in an operator UI without the same security controls as the main path.

Test malformed bytes, incompatible schema, permanent domain rejection, dependency outage, handler bug, batch partial failure and replay after the original state has changed.

The full broker guidance is (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q5), with deduplication in (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q6).
:::

items.q: RabbitMQ Publisher Confirms: three modes and ConcurrentSkipListMap
Cache stampede (thundering herd)
items.a:
A hot key expires → thousands of requests miss simultaneously → all hit the database together → a [[r:lethal load spike]].

- [[b:Single-flight / mutex]]: allow only one request to rebuild the entry using a `setnx` lock with a TTL; all other requests wait and read again
- [[b:XFetch]] (probabilistic early expiration): each request has a small probability of rebuilding *before* expiration → there is no single instant when every request misses
- [[b:Logical expiration]]: never let the key physically expire; after its logical expiry, one request rebuilds it in the background while all others receive the stale value → nobody waits, at the cost of accepting staleness

:::deep
Logical expiration suits data that tolerates staleness, such as a displayed exchange rate; single-flight suits data that must be fresh but can tolerate waiting.

[[r:Fintech balances should not use simple cache-aside]]. A lock needs a TTL so the cache does not deadlock if the lock holder dies; also beware of the lock itself becoming a hot key → add a local L1 cache.
:::

items.q: Hot keys
items.a:
One extremely hot key concentrates traffic on a single Redis node, causing a [[r:bottleneck while the rest of the cluster is idle]] because sharding assigns that key to one slot.

- [[b:L1 (Caffeine) + L2 (Redis)]]: a short L1 TTL keeps most reads away from Redis
- [[b:Synthetic key replication]]: write `key#1..key#N` and choose a replica randomly on reads → spread load across multiple slots, at the cost of more complex invalidation

:::deep
L1+L2+DB is a standard production hierarchy: The L1 hit ratio is workload-specific; measure it by key class and include invalidation traffic, memory pressure, cold starts, and stale-read cost before sizing Redis.

The [[r:cost]] is distributed invalidation. When data changes, the L1 entry must be removed from *every* instance using Redis pub/sub, or the system must accept a short TTL. Detect hot keys with Redis `--hotkeys` and client-side sampling.

Because hot keys can appear suddenly during events such as flash sales, mature systems need automatic detection and dynamic promotion into L1.
:::

items.q: Cache penetration
items.a:
[[b:Cache penetration]] is repeated lookup of keys that do not exist or are not visible to the caller, so every request bypasses the positive cache and reaches the source of truth. It may come from normal misses, stale links, enumeration attacks, or a client bug.

- Validate key shape and authorization before expensive lookup; apply per-principal/tenant/IP risk-based rate limits rather than trusting cache defenses alone.
- Negative-cache “not found” with a bounded, jittered TTL and a key that includes every authorization/tenant dimension. Invalidate or version it when creation can make the key valid. Bound cache size so attacker-generated junk cannot evict useful data.
- A Bloom filter can reject definite non-members with compact memory. Standard Bloom filters allow false positives but not false negatives [[o:only while the filter correctly represents all inserted valid keys]]; stale construction or missed updates can violate the application's assumption.
- Size it from expected cardinality and target false-positive rate.

:::deep
For high-churn/deletion workloads, rebuilding, partitioning by generation, a counting filter, or a Cuckoo filter may fit better; each adds update and consistency complexity.

A filter also reveals nothing about authorization and should not become a side channel for whether another tenant's object exists.

Observe negative-cache insert/hit/eviction, filter saturation/false-positive estimates, source lookup rate and top bounded rejection classes. Test create-after-negative-cache, tenant crossover, random-key flood, filter lag and source outage.

The broader cache strategy is (10-system-design-rate-limit.framework-building-blocks.q3).
:::

items.q: Cache avalanches and invalidation
items.a:
- [[b:Avalanche]]: many keys with the same TTL expire together → a load spike. Fix it with [[g:TTL jitter]] such as `base + random(0, base*0.2)`
- [[b:Invalidation]]: after writing the database, [[g:delete the key]] rather than updating it → avoid a race in which an older value overwrites the new cached value

:::deep
A [[r:rare delete race]] remains: a read misses → loads an old value → a concurrent write updates the database and deletes the key → the read writes the old value back into the cache.

Mitigate it with [[g:delayed double-delete]]—delete, write the database, wait a few hundred milliseconds, then delete again—or with a short TTL.

The [[o:golden rule for fintech]] is not to cache balances or limits with plain cache-aside. If caching is unavoidable, use versioning or push updates through CDC.
:::

items.q: The read-path patterns: cache-aside, read-through, refresh-ahead
items.a: All six cache patterns answer one question: [[o:who writes the entry, and when]]. On the read path that narrows to who handles a miss — the application, the cache itself, or a background worker. **1 · Cache-aside (lazy loading)** — the application asks the cache; on a miss it reads the database and writes the value back itself. - [[g:Why it is the default]]: the cache is optional. Lose it and every read still answers, only slower, and nothing in the write path changes. - [[r:What it costs]]: a miss is three hops instead of one, the first read of a key is always slow, and the get/set logic ends up copied to every call site. - Fits reads that dominate writes and data that may be stale for the length of the TTL. **2 · Read-through** — the application only ever talks to the cache; a loader inside the cache reads the database on a miss and stores the result. - [[g:What you gain]]: one place owns loading, so no call site can forget the `set` or invent its own key format. - [[r:What it costs]]: you need a cache that supports loaders, lookups are by key only — no joins, no dynamic filters — and the cache is now on the critical path of every read. **3 · Refresh-ahead** — a worker reloads a key before its TTL runs out, so no reader ever pays for the reload. - [[g:What you gain]]: miss latency disappears for the keys it covers, and a hot key stops being a stampede trigger (25-microservice.05-caching-pitfalls.q1). - [[r:What it costs]]: it is a guess. Refreshing a key nobody reads spends a database query on nothing, so it pays only where the hot set is known — a campaign, a flash sale, a home page. :::tip A hit costs the same in all three They differ in who owns the miss, not in speed. What changes is where the loading code lives and what the system does when the cache is gone. ::: :::deep - Spring's `@Cacheable` [[o:looks read-through but is cache-aside]]: the proxy does the get and set around your method, so a cache outage surfaces inside your code, and `sync = true` is its single-flight switch (03-spring-boot-deep-build.ioc-container-transactions.q6). - Caffeine's `LoadingCache` is real read-through in-process, and it collapses concurrent misses on one key into a single load while the rest wait — the stampede fix arrives with the pattern (25-microservice.05-caching-pitfalls.q1). - `refreshAfterWrite` is refresh-ahead in one line: the first read after the refresh point starts a reload in the background and still returns the old value. - read-through against a remote cache makes that cache a hard dependency. Decide fail-open or fail-closed per use, and decide it together with where L1 and L2 live (10-system-design-rate-limit.framework-building-blocks.q6). :::

items.q: The write-path patterns: write-through, write-behind, write-around
items.a: On a write the question is whether the cache sits on the path at all, and whether the database write happens inside the request. **4 · Write-through** — the write goes to the cache and the database in one synchronous flow, and the client waits for both. - [[g:What you gain]]: a read straight after a write never sees the old value, and there is no separate invalidation step to forget. - [[r:What it costs]]: every write pays both latencies, and the cache fills up with values nobody reads. **5 · Write-behind (write-back)** — the cache acknowledges the write immediately and a worker flushes to the database later, in batches. - [[g:What you gain]]: the highest write throughput of the six; a thousand increments of one counter collapse into one row update. - [[r:What it costs]]: a real loss window. This is the only pattern of the six where an acknowledged write can disappear. **6 · Write-around** — the write goes straight to the database and the key is deleted from the cache; the next read reloads it. - [[g:What you gain]]: write-once-read-never data never occupies cache memory, which keeps the hot set resident. - [[r:What it costs]]: the read right after a write is guaranteed to miss, and a forgotten delete leaves a stale entry until the TTL expires. **What people actually run:** - Ordinary read-heavy service: [[b:cache-aside + write-around]] — read lazily, write the database, delete the key. Cheapest to operate, and correct as long as the delete happens after the commit (25-microservice.05-caching-pitfalls.q4). - Large read volume over a small hot set, such as a flash sale or a home page: add [[b:refresh-ahead]] or logical expiry so the hot key never expires under load. - Counters, view counts, metrics, logs: [[b:write-behind]] with a bounded buffer and a loss window someone has agreed to. :::warn Write-behind is the one pattern that can lose an acknowledged write The client is told 200 before the row exists, so the loss window is the flush interval plus the buffer depth. Keep it away from balances, orders and ledger entries; use it where a lost increment is a rounding error. ::: :::deep - write-through is [[r:not a transaction]]: two stores, two writes. Decide what the code does when the second one fails — this is the dual-write problem in another costume (25-microservice.03-distributed-data-consistency.q1). - on invalidation, delete the key instead of writing the new value into it; two concurrent writers can otherwise leave the older value sitting in the cache (25-microservice.05-caching-pitfalls.q4). - write-behind's durability is the buffer's durability. An in-process buffer loses everything on a crash, Redis AOF with `everysec` can still lose about a second of writes, and the durable version is a log the worker consumes. - write-around plus a short TTL is the honest version of "the delete can fail": the delete is best-effort and the TTL is the backstop. :::

items.q: Two sizing mistakes that turn the cache into the incident
items.a:
A cache does not make a system faster; it moves the load elsewhere and adds a second copy of the truth. Two decisions settle whether that trade pays: how long an entry lives, and which entries are let in at all.

**Mistake 1 — a short TTL on a hot key.** TTL is a [[o:staleness budget]], not a performance knob. A key read 5,000 times a second with a 30-second TTL schedules a stampede every 30 seconds: at expiry every in-flight request misses together and the database takes the full read rate.

- Changing the number is not the fix. Five seconds makes it worse and five minutes only moves it; what has to change is that expiry stops being a cliff — single-flight, logical expiry, or refresh-ahead (25-microservice.05-caching-pitfalls.q1).
- Give every TTL jitter so keys loaded together do not expire together (25-microservice.05-caching-pitfalls.q4).

**Mistake 2 — writing every key you happen to read into the cache.** An entry earns its memory by being read again before it changes or expires.

Cache everything and the working set outgrows the memory: eviction starts, entries that were about to be reused get dropped, and the hit rate collapses while memory reads 100%.

- Decide per key class, not per endpoint. A product page is read thousands of times; an audit record is read once and belongs in the database only — which is exactly what write-around is for.
- Size it from the real thing: `MEMORY USAGE <key>` on a representative key, times the number you intend to keep resident, then leave headroom for fragmentation and replication buffers.
- `maxmemory-policy` is a product decision, not a default. `noeviction` turns a full cache into write errors, `allkeys-lru` keeps it behaving as a cache, and `allkeys-lfu` protects a small hot set from a scan.
- Admission and the real engine algorithms are compared in (25-microservice.05-caching-pitfalls.q10).

**Read the hit rate per key class, never globally.** One class at 99% and one at 20% average out to a number that looks healthy, while the second class is the one arriving at the database.

:::deep
- eviction is not expiry: an entry can vanish long before its TTL, so no correctness rule may assume it is still there. Idempotency keys kept only in a cache are the classic version of this bug (25-microservice.09-idempotency-the-central-link.q1).
- by tier, for a read-heavy service: at T1–T2 (10k–100k req/day, ~2.5–25 rps peak) a cache is `not needed` — the missing index is usually the real fix; at T3 (1M req/day, ~250 rps peak) it is `worth it`.
- at T4 (100M req/day, ~25,000 rps peak) the cache is `mandatory`, and the hot set `needs its own scaling story`: an L1 in front of exactly those keys, not a larger Redis (25-microservice.05-caching-pitfalls.q2).
- measure the cost of a miss, not the hit rate alone: 95% hits with a two-second miss is worse at p99 than 80% hits with a 40 ms miss.
- a cold start after a deploy or a failover is the same event as a mass expiry. Warm the keys you know are hot, or admit misses gradually with a bounded rebuild concurrency (10-system-design-rate-limit.framework-building-blocks.q3).
:::

items.q: Redis beyond the cache: which structure answers which problem
items.a:
Redis is a server of data structures with expiry, and its data path executes one command at a time — which is why every single command is already atomic. That one sentence is the reason it ends up doing a dozen jobs; the real question is which of them it is allowed to own.
JobStructure and commandsWhat it costs you

Distributed lockSET key token NX PX ttl, released by a Lua compare-and-deletethe TTL can expire mid-work, so the resource needs a fencing token
(09-distributed-tx-fintech.distributed-transaction-patterns.q6)

the database constraint stays the real guarantee (25-microservice.09-idempotency-the-central-link.q1)
